topic: Rust versus Go for high-throughput network services: performance, memory safety, concurrency model and ecosystem trade-offs

key_points.point: Rust has no garbage collector: ownership and borrowing are enforced at compile time and memory is freed deterministically at scope end, avoiding GC cost and use-after-free/double-free bugs outside unsafe code.
Go uses a concurrent, non-moving tracing mark-sweep GC; GOGC (default 100) trades memory for CPU, and GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+) sets a soft memory cap.

Go GC pauses are short and mostly independent of heap size (historically sub-millisecond; 500 microsecond stop-the-world goal), but GC still costs CPU, assists and write barriers that can affect tail latency.

Discord's Read States service had Go latency spikes about every 2 minutes from forced GC scanning a large LRU cache; the Rust port removed spikes and beat Go on latency, CPU and memory (2019, Go 1.9.2 era).

Cloudflare's Rust proxy Pingora used about 70% less CPU and 67% less memory than the prior NGINX/Lua-based service, partly from architecture changes (shared connection pools, multithreading), not language alone.

Go concurrency is built-in: lightweight goroutines scheduled by the runtime with channels (CSP style); Rust async needs a runtime crate such as Tokio, uses explicit await, and futures do nothing until awaited.
Go does not prevent data races (they can cause crashes and memory corruption); the race detector finds them only at runtime on executed paths, with 5-10x memory and 2-20x time overhead.
Memory-safe languages reduce vulnerabilities: Android's memory-safety bug share fell from 76% (2019) to 24% (2024) as new code shifted to memory-safe languages including Rust.

Tokio offers a multi-threaded work-stealing scheduler suited to IO-bound workloads; it is not advised for CPU-bound parallelism (rayon instead), and async Rust still has rough edges (async traits, destruction).

Rust memory guarantees do not cover unsafe code, and Discord noted early async Rust needed nightly and had boilerplate-heavy, hard-to-read errors; the authors did not advocate rewriting everything in Rust.
Go's GC can be tuned (GOGC, GOMEMLIMIT, fewer allocations, escape-analysis checks) to cut GC cost, so GC-driven latency gaps depend on workload and tuning; claims should rest on measured benchmarks.
